candidates.title: Project Helix’s Design is Being Informed by Backwards Compatibility, Says VP of Next-Gen
candidates.excerpt: While Microsoft has made several strides when it comes to making older games playable on its current-gen consoles, the company seems to have plans regarding game preservation with its next-gen console – Project Helix. Xbox’s VP of Next Generation, Jason Ronald, discussed this in an interview on page 17 of the Xbox 25th Anniversary magazine, where he said that “game preservation is core to Xbox.” The big reason behind this, Ronald explained, is due to Microsoft’s position as one of the biggest publishers and platforms in the industry. This gives the company a “deep responsibility” to make sure that the history of gaming isn’t forgotten due to changing hardware. While noting that the industry has traditionally been quite bad at preserving its works, more recently, older games have started becoming much more accessible to even console gamers. “For the first 30 years of game development, nobody really thought about game preservation when they were designing their hardware, when they were building their games. “A great example of where that’s already starting to happen today came earlier this year. For the first time ever, I can now play original Xbox games on my PC and a handheld. When those games were originally designed, and when we designed the original Xbox, we never envisioned a future where that could actually be true.” Looking to the future, Project Helix will seemingly be designed with game preservation and backwards compatibility in mind. candidates.title: Xbox Project Helix Is A Console That Plays PC Games, Not The Other Way Around
candidates.excerpt: Xbox has revealed more details about its next-gen device, Project Helix, describing it as a "console capable of playing games from your PC." Prominently featured in the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine, VP of next-gen Jason Ronald said the Xbox Series X|S successor is designed to build on the successes — and hard lessons — of previous Xbox generations, with fewer barriers to play. "When we think about Project Helix, it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine--one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed," Ronald said. "My entire library is accessible to me. I'm able to bring four generations of my Xbox library and progression with me and have it available instantly. And we remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games." Ronald added that the Project Helix family of devices isn't purely focused on traditional next-gen themes like better graphics, but on thinking ahead to create "innovative" experiences. "We don't think the next generation is defined by 8K, or 240 hertz, or some of the traditional metrics--it's really about gameplay innovation," Ronald explained. "We're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games.
